articles.title: Enabling automatic transcription of child-centered audio recordings from real-world environments
articles.authors: Daniil Kocharov, Azarias Galama, Okko Räsänen
articles.abstract: Longform audio recordings obtained with microphones worn by children—also known as child-centered daylong recordings—have become a standard method for studying children’s language experiences and their impact on subsequent language development. Transcripts of longform speech audio would enable rich analyses at various linguistic levels, yet the massive scale of typical longform corpora prohibits comprehensive manual annotation. Meanwhile, automatic speech recognition (ASR)-based transcription faces significant challenges due to the noisy, unconstrained nature of real-world audio. Previous attempts have assumed that ASR must process each longform recording in its entirety. In this work, we present an approach for automatic detection of those utterances in longform audio that can be reliably transcribed with modern ASR systems, allowing automatic and relatively accurate transcription of a notable proportion of all speech in typical longform data. We validate the approach on four English longform corpora, showing that it achieves a median word error rate (WER) of 0% and a mean WER of 16% when transcribing 30% of the total speech in the dataset. In contrast, transcribing all speech without any filtering yields a median WER of 52% and a mean WER of 51%. We also compare word log-frequencies derived from the automatic transcripts with those from manual annotations and show that the frequencies correlate at r = 0.94 (Pearson) for all transcribed words and r = 0.99 for words that appear at least five times in the automatic transcripts. Overall, the work provides a concrete step toward increasingly detailed automated linguistic analyses of child-centered longform audio.

articles.title: Antiracism Self-Efficacy: Motivating Individuals Toward Racial Justice
articles.authors: Kristin A. Broussard, Narda R. Quigley, Holly Slay Ferraro, Seth Matthew Fishman, Amanda M. Grannas, Teresa A. Nance, Teresa M. Boyer, Noelle K. Comolli, Elizabeth M. Svenson, Adam R. Smith, Adriana Reilly, Kamil Vickers
articles.abstract: We integrate existing research on racial justice allyship and antiracism with social cognitive theory to develop our understanding of why and how individuals who identify as White in the context of the US may initiate and sustain antiracist behavior at the individual level. In Study 1a, we define the concept of antiracism self-efficacy and develop a seven-item measure. We then examine the extent to which the seven-item scale exhibits convergent and discriminant validity in Study 1b. In Study 2, we demonstrate that antiracism self-efficacy predicts a broad range of antiracist behavioral intentions and behaviors above and beyond racial attitudes and beliefs. Study 3 extends this argument using a bias-confrontation paradigm, demonstrating that antiracism self-efficacy predicts bias-confrontation outcomes above and beyond other motivational constructs and general self-efficacy. Overall, this work identifies and explores antiracism self-efficacy as an important concept that motivates individuals toward racial justice allyship and antiracist behavior at a micro (i.e., day-to-day) level. We posit that including antiracism self-efficacy in motivational models addressing allyship and antiracist behavior will help guide future empirical work on antiracism at the individual level, in addition to having important practical implications for racial justice/antiracism education, training, and other related initiatives within organizations.

articles.title: Detecting Careless Responding: A Comparison of Norm Group-Based Mahalanobis Distance and Norm Group-Based Person-Total Correlation with Their Sample-Based Counterparts
articles.authors: Philippe Goldammer, Yannik A. Escher, Peter Lucas Stöckli, Hubert Annen, Anna Luca Heimann
articles.abstract: Detecting careless responding in self-report questionnaires has gained considerable attention. Different detection methods have been proposed, with implicit methods offering clear advantages over explicit ones. Mahalanobis distance (MD) and person-total correlation ( r pbis ) are among the most promising implicit detection methods. However, previous research has suggested that MD and r pbis are less accurate indicators of careless responding when the percentage of careless respondents in the sample is high and that norm group-based (NGB) MD and r pbis might be more accurate alternatives under that condition. In two simulation studies and a reanalysis of real data, we examined whether NGB MD and NGB r pbis indeed outperform their sample-based (SB) counterparts in a variety of careless responding patterns. The three main findings were as follows: (1) NGB MD outperformed SB MD in most conditions in three studies, (2) both MD indices (but not r pbis indices) were ineffective when simulated scale-midpoint invariant and full straightlining careless responding had to be detected, and (3) NGB r pbis almost never outperformed SB r pbis . We therefore recommend using NGB MD instead of SB MD, and using SB r pbis instead of NGB r pbis when screening data for careless responding.

articles.title: Inferring Struggle, Judging Strength: How Inferred Adversity and Sympathy Shape Competence Evaluations of Black Frontline Employees
articles.authors: Shahin Sharifi
articles.abstract: How do racial inferences shape third-party evaluations of employee competence? Across four experiments, White U.S. observers judged Black frontline employees as more competent than otherwise comparable White employees in service-failure encounters involving a Black customer. This pattern was consistent with a serial process in which employee race cued greater inferred adversity, which elicited sympathy, thereby elevating competence judgments. Study 1 established the competence difference and its association with lower negative word of mouth. Study 2 showed that behavioral awkwardness attenuated the difference. Study 3 supported the serial indirect pathway, and the supplementary pilot reproduced it without a service failure. Study 4 showed that structural-opportunity information increased inferred adversity for both employees and especially increased sympathy and competence judgments for the White employee, narrowing Black–White differences. The findings identify a context-dependent, normatively complex route through which presumed adversity can produce comparatively favorable yet racialized competence judgments.

articles.title: Helpful and in Danger: Attributes and Correlates of Perceived Occupational Heroism
articles.authors: Jean Monéger, Roger Giner-Sorolla
articles.abstract: Some occupations such as firefighters are described as heroic, while others, such as healthcare workers, are applauded as “heroes” in crises. In two preregistered correlational studies conducted on representative U.K. samples, we evaluated theory-based attributes of occupational heroism, and its relationship to specific policy-relevant attitudes toward occupations. In Study 1 ( N = 430), we confirmed that occupational heroism relates to the perceived helpfulness and risk exposure of workers. In Study 2 ( N = 840), we further showed that occupational heroism is associated with a moral shield: workers’ hero status correlates with decreased acceptability of criticism toward them, and increased support for deregulating them and protecting them from punishment for rule-breaking. Unlike previous findings suggesting a willingness to exploit heroized workers, heroism correlated with increased gratitude toward workers, support for their demands, and perception that they are vulnerable. Societal consequences and relevance for policy-making are discussed.

articles.title: Context Matters, Doesn’t It? The Role of Context in Everyday Emotion Regulation Strategy Use
articles.authors: Anh Tran, Rachel Freeman-Robinson, Peter Koval, Katharine H. Greenaway, Elise K. Kalokerinos
articles.abstract: A common maxim holds that “context is everything.” This perspective transformed the field of emotion regulation, which evolved from understanding which regulation strategies people use, to understanding how strategy use varies by context (i.e., strategy–situation fit). Theoretical accounts suggest contextual features are crucial in guiding strategy use. However, empirical evidence is isolated in piecemeal studies with inconclusive results. To comprehensively explore context-dependent emotion regulation, we need data on emotion regulation across many contexts, at scale. Combining up to 11 experience-sampling data sets collected from Belgian and Australian samples in an integrative analysis ( N ID = 500–1,696, N observations = 27,023–101,114, M age = 25.38 years, 71% women), we examined how regulation-strategy use varies as a function of three theory-derived contextual features— intensity , controllability , and social features (i.e., the presence and closeness of others). We found limited support that context matters for daily emotion-regulation strategy use. Our study provides a well-powered foundational step to test a theory central to emotion-regulation research and highlights the complexity of capturing strategy–situation fit in daily life.

articles.title: High School Music Participation: The Role of Identity, Value, Expectancy, and Cost
articles.authors: Seth Pendergast, Peter Miksza
articles.abstract: While secondary music programs enjoy participation from many students, school music enrollment often does not reflect the demographics of the broader student population. This study examined how high-school students’ musical identities and sociocognitive beliefs influenced their intentions to enroll in high-school music classes. Drawing on situated expectancy-value theory, we developed a model of how musical identity and expectancy-value constructs influence students’ enrollment decisions in three music classes: large ensembles, music technology/production, and piano/guitar. We surveyed 486 students at a large U.S. public high school, measuring musical identity, expectancy-value constructs, and intentions to enroll in each of the three class contexts. Structural equation models showed musical identity positively predicted expectancy and value; expectancy negatively predicted cost; and both value and cost predicted enrollment intentions (positively and negatively, respectively). Notably, expectancy influenced intentions only indirectly via cost. Although both value and cost predicted intentions across all class types, cost was more strongly associated with intentions for large ensembles, whereas value was more strongly associated with intentions for music technology/production and piano/guitar. These findings suggest motivational beliefs are context-dependent and deeply interrelated. Music teachers may benefit from considering the context-specific roles of cost, value, and expectancy when recruiting students for classes.

articles.title: Expressive Priority and Goal Structure and Complexity During Collegiate, Faculty, and Professional Chamber Music Rehearsals
articles.authors: Rebecca A. Roesler, Robin S. Heinsen, Laura K. Hicken
articles.abstract: The purpose of this study was to discover the artistic conceptualizations and priorities of collegiate, faculty, and professional musicians during the moment-to-moment decision-making of a rehearsal. We utilized musicians’ verbalizations during chamber music rehearsals as a vehicle for exploring their thought processes. Analysis 1 investigated the rehearsal targets ensembles prioritized as a percentage of total rehearsal time allocated to each. Analysis 2 investigated the complexity and form of professional, faculty, and collegiate chamber musicians’ goal structures as they attended to musical targets in relation to one another. Professional chamber ensembles prioritized the expressive targets of character and phrasing above all others, and significantly more as a percentage of rehearsal time than did collegiate chamber ensembles. Goal complexity increased with each level of experience from collegiate to professional ensembles; faculty and professional ensembles pursued elemental and technical goals in service of paramount expressive ends such as character and phrasing. We discuss the possible causes for this phenomenon, implications for music education, and recommendations for further research in these areas. We also recommend that teachers consider crafting music learning experiences to facilitate learners’ focus on expressive ends and pursual of proximal goals in service of artistic aims.

articles.title: Living Criteria: Co-Construction of Evaluative Criteria in Creative Collaboration in the Primary Classroom
articles.authors: Ashleigh Southam, Aleksandra Getman
articles.abstract: Research with both professional musicians and children shows that during creativity, evaluations – such as liking, novelty and structure – shape decision-making. Less is known about how these evaluative processes operate in collaborative classroom settings where creativity also supports learning. This study examined how primary school students evaluate ideas during collaborative creative tasks, particularly in relation to their musical decisions. A qualitative case study was conducted with 18 students (aged 9–10) in a primary classroom across five integrated arts lessons centred on composing and performing rhythmic ostinati. Classroom observations, peer-feedback forms and student interviews were analysed thematically. Findings showed that students co-constructed a ‘Living Criteria’: a shared, dynamic evaluative system guiding idea generation, selection and refinement. This system comprised three components: Task-Specific Congruence (judging ideas by task fit and clarity), Emerging Aesthetic Evaluation (linking humour, enjoyment and ‘liking’ with perceived quality) and Collaborative Sensitivity (balancing idea quality with group harmony). Although limited by its small sample and single-class context, the study demonstrates how children integrate aesthetic, practical and social considerations when working together musically and creatively. The concept of ‘Living Criteria’ offers a framework for understanding how evaluative judgement develops through collaboration, with implications for music pedagogy and creative learning research.

articles.title: Exploring Musicians’ Perspectives on Decent Work, Creativity, and Well-Being
articles.authors: Liliana Faria, Ana Martins
articles.abstract: This study, grounded in the psychology of working theory (PWT) and self-determination theory (SDT), examined how working conditions shape musicians’ experiences of decent work, intrinsic motivation, artistic identity, creative engagement, and psychological well-being. Sixteen in-depth interviews were conducted with Portuguese musicians, including both freelancers and those with stable contracts. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four overarching themes: (a) job security and precarity, (b) intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and creative engagement, (c) artistic identity and purpose, and (d) well-being and mental health. The findings show that freelance instability undermines security, constrains creative risk-taking, and increases stress, whereas financial and institutional stability supports intrinsic motivation, reinforces artistic identity, and enables creative exploration. Features associated with intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement, persistence, and psychological investment in creative tasks were observed across both groups. Autonomy itself sustained engagement for some freelancers, highlighting personal resilience and self-directed creativity. The results underscore the interplay between structural conditions (PWT) and individual motivations (SDT), showing that sustainable work environments foster well-being and high-quality creative output. The study provides practical implications for policies, education, and organizational strategies to support healthier, more productive artistic ecosystems.

articles.title: Does Self-Compassion Moderate the Association Between Music-Specific Stress and Internalizing Symptoms?
articles.authors: Darya Ellalasingham, Ishan N. Vengurlekar, Christopher J. McCarthy
articles.abstract: Music students are a high-risk population for mental health challenges due to the unique sources of stress they encounter. Previous work indicates that these music-specific stressors are associated with higher levels of internalizing symptoms (i.e., depression and anxiety). Consequently, further attention to protective assets and resources for music students is crucial. One construct that has garnered attention from scholars is self-compassion. Prior studies have documented benefits of self-compassion in reducing and attenuating the link between stress and internalizing symptoms. Yet, no study to date has considered whether self-compassion and its six subscales moderate the association between music-study stress and internalizing symptoms. The current study explored whether self-compassion and its six subcomponents moderate the relationship between music-study stress and internalizing symptoms among student musicians. Participants were 151 music students at a public university in the United States. We found a positive association between music-study stress and internalizing symptoms. In addition, results revealed that self-judgment and isolation moderated the link between music-study stress and anxious symptoms, such that at higher levels of self-judgment and isolation, music-study stress evinced stronger associations with anxious symptoms than at lower levels of the two. We discuss the rationales for our findings and practice implications.

articles.title: Mental Health Implications of (Mal-)Adaptive Approaches to Leisure Music Engagement: The Role of Motivation and Self-Criticism
articles.authors: Friederike Koehler, Julia Vigl, Suvi Saarikallio
articles.abstract: The relationship between music engagement and health has attracted growing academic interest over the past decades, pointing to mostly beneficial associations, especially with music listening and music interventions. However, recent research indicates a more complex relationship emphasizing the relevance of exploring how and why people engage with music. Since playing music and singing are common leisure-time activities for many people, this study aimed to investigate potential (mal-)adaptive approaches to music engagement, that is, self-determined motivation, and its association with mental health in amateur musicians. One hundred and ninety-eight participants completed an online survey on their motivation to make music, as well as depression, anxiety, stress, and self-criticism. Structural equation models showed that controlled motivation (more external reasons) positively predicted depression, stress, and self-criticism, but not anxiety. Further, results provided evidence for a full mediation of the association between controlled motivation and depression, anxiety, and stress via self-criticism. Our findings highlight the importance of individual motivations and dispositions in music engagement, pointing to potentially harmful effects on mental health. Practical implications for effective health promotion include considering individual motivations and dispositions and enhancing autonomy and self-compassion in leisure interventions and recreational therapy. Future research should investigate further individual and situational determinants.

articles.title: Implications of Self-Recording of Audition Performances in Opera Singers: A Multiple Case Study
articles.authors: Melissa Treinkman
articles.abstract: This qualitative multiple case study investigated the potential benefits of audio self-recording during university opera auditions. While commonly employed in individual practice, self-recording remains rare in formal audition settings, possibly hindering performers’ ability to critically evaluate their performance. Five classical university voice students participated in semi-structured interviews after completing an audio-recorded opera audition. Each student reflected on the audition both before and after listening to their recording. Thematic analysis revealed the following three primary themes: (a) self-recording as a tool for recalling specific details of the audition, (b) shifts in self-perception after listening, and (c) reduced post-audition rumination. These findings underscore the need for further research and highlight the potential of audio self-recording as a cost-effective, pedagogically valuable intervention that may support reflective learning, emotional regulation, and more effective audition preparation within higher education settings.

articles.title: A Lasting Impression: Performance Memory Persists After a Single Musical Exposure
articles.authors: David Duncan, Katya Ness, Ian Cross
articles.abstract: Despite the centrality of memory to music reading and performance, little is known about incidental long-term memory retention of music that is performed at sight. In this study, 19 undergraduate pianists sight-read a series of short, unfamiliar pieces, and then returned 1–3 weeks later to perform the same pieces, without opportunities to see or practise the music in the interim. Pitch, rhythm, and metre errors were all found to decrease in the second reading, with error counts dropping on average by 13% from Reading 1 to Reading 2, while error types and sizes tended to persist across readings. No significant differences were found between those who had a 1-, 2-, or 3-week gap between readings, suggesting that a single brief encounter with a score can have a long-term priming effect. These findings illustrate how robust musical memory can be and may have implications for our understanding of how motor and memory systems support long-term retention in skilled performance.
